entry.title: Safer: Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community

media:group.media:title: Safer: Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community
media:group.media:description:
• Presented by the Bloomberg School of Public Health and Hopkins at Home • • Featuring Raj Panjabi, BSPH '06 (MPH), Dean Sarah Szanton, and Lisa Cooper •
When crisis strikes — a diagnosis, a natural disaster, a sudden upheaval at work or at home — our instinct is to pull inward. But as Hopkins alumnus Dr. Raj Panjabi argues in his new book, Safer: A Playbook—Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community, isolation is the wrong instinct. Connection is the real protection.
Dr. Panjabi has spent his career on the front lines of crisis: fleeing civil war in Liberia as a child, building community health systems as founding CEO of Last Mile Health, and steering the nation's pandemic response as White House Senior Director for Global Health Security. In Safer, he distills that experience into a practical roadmap — eight "plays" for navigating fear, cutting through misinformation, and rebuilding trust in divided times.
Joining Dr. Panjabi for this conversation are two Johns Hopkins leaders whose own work embodies the book's central idea — that community, not isolation, is what keeps us safe. Sarah Szanton, Dean of the Johns Hopkins School of Nursing, is the architect of CAPABLE, a program that has helped thousands of older adults age safely in their own communities rather than in isolation. Lisa Cooper, the James F. Fries Professor of Medicine and a Bloomberg Distinguished Professor across Hopkins' Schools of Medicine, Nursing, and Public Health, has spent her career studying how trust between patients, physicians, and communities determines who stays healthy — and who doesn't.
Together, our speakers explore what it really takes to turn fear into action and crisis into community, both in our health systems and in our daily lives.
#johnshopkinsuniversity @JohnsHopkinsSPH #booktalk #rajpanjabi #sarahszanton #lisacooper #publichealth

media:group.media:title: Arts & Archives: DIY Publishing
media:group.media:description:
A conversation on the art of independent publishing in Baltimore, featuring three voices shaping the city's DIY print culture: - Jess Jess Press, a comic and magazine press specializing in Risograph printing with a focus on publishing marginalized authors and artists. - Momo Mullings, a Baltimore-based writer, artist, organizer, and archivist whose work spans zines, performance, and publishing. - Cara Ober, founding editor and publisher of BmoreArt, a platform for creative and critical discussion and a leading resource for contemporary art and culture in Baltimore.
Set against the backdrop of the Peabody Library's historic atrium, this event put materials from the Sheridan Libraries' archives and special collections in dialogue with the speakers, exploring how independent presses and community publishing shape and preserve artistic voices in Baltimore.
The discussion was moderated by Nate Brown, coordinator of Johns Hopkins' Common Question initiative, which this year asks: "What Is Art?" It is co-sponsored by the Winston Tabb Special Collections Research Center and the Common Question.
#johnshopkinsuniversity @JHULibraries #diypublishing #zines #independentpress

entry.title: A New Era for the Johns Hopkins Homewood Campus

media:group.media:title: A New Era for the Johns Hopkins Homewood Campus
media:group.media:description:
Construction on the new AMR I Residence Hall & Dining Replacement Project has already begun, but a symbolic groundbreaking celebration recently took place to mark the first new housing and dining project in forty years on the Johns Hopkins University Homewood campus. Speakers included a current resident advisor and leadership from the university who took to the stage to discuss what this new residence hall and dining facility will mean to students of the future. The new facility will provide 120,000 square feet of living space for 400 first-year students, which doubles the capacity of the previous AMR I. With these updated facilities comes new possibilities: new spaces to connect, work together, and thrive.
Video by: Aubrey Morse

entry.title: For Every Next First: The Campaign for Johns Hopkins

media:group.media:title: For Every Next First: The Campaign for Johns Hopkins
media:group.media:description: Since our founding in 1876 as America’s first research university, Johns Hopkins has been dedicated to creating new knowledge and bringing the benefits of those discoveries to the world. From the introduction of rubber gloves for surgery and the invention of CPR to the first American university press, and the first full color image of Earth, we have a long history of firsts of which to be proud. For Every Next First: The Campaign for Johns Hopkins is not about where we’ve been. It’s about where we’re going and what together we can make possible. Visit giving.jhu.edu to learn more.

entry.title: SNF Agora Institute: AI and the Future of History

media:group.media:title: SNF Agora Institute: AI and the Future of History
media:group.media:description:
Presented by Hopkins at Home, the SNF Agora Institute, and the Data Science and AI Institute at Johns Hopkins University
What does it mean for a democracy when most people ask AI what really happened? As in most fields, AI is rapidly transforming how history is taught, researched, and understood. Professor Hyman discusses the exciting ways that AI promises to advance research, by unlocking the histories hidden in archives, even as it is changing how history is taught, and ultimately, how we understand the past itself.
Louis Hyman, the Dorothy Ross Professor of History, teaches “Introduction to Computational History” and, in addition to SNF Agora, is also a faculty member of the Data Science and AI Institute.

entry.title: Building Winning Teams: Championship Culture | Johns Hopkins Athletics

media:group.media:title: Building Winning Teams: Championship Culture | Johns Hopkins Athletics
media:group.media:description:
• Presented by Johns Hopkins University Athletics and Hopkins at Home • • Featuring head coaches Peter Milliman, Dan Wodicka, and Tim McCormack •
Great teams don’t happen by chance—they are built with purpose, trust, resilience, and a shared commitment to something greater. What separates a collection of talented individuals from a truly great team? Winning organizations aren’t built on talent alone. They require trust, shared purpose, accountability, and a culture in which everyone understands how their individual contributions support a larger goal.
Drawing on their experiences leading nationally competitive programs, coaches across Johns Hopkins University Athletics foster a collaborative, winning spirit among their teams. Our featured head coaches discuss how they establish expectations, create buy-in, balance individual excellence with team goals, develop leadership throughout an organization, and maintain a strong culture through both success and adversity.
Joining us for this conversation are: - Peter Milliman, Alexander Kuehl ’66 Head Coach of Men’s Lacrosse - Dan Wodicka, James F. Margraff Head Coach of Football - Tim McCormack, Head Women’s Lacrosse Coach
Whether you’re leading a team, contributing to one, or simply interested in what makes high-performing groups thrive, this conversation will offer practical insights into creating an environment where people can succeed together.
#johnshopkins @HopkinsSports #athletics #coaching #teamculture
